html:
A collection of Siamese laws put together in 1805 on the orders of King Rama I. It was the working law of Siam for a century, until modern codes replaced it in the early 20th century.

Most of the old law books had been lost when the Burmese destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, in the Burmese Siamese war. The story goes that in 1804 a woman won a divorce though she was the one at fault, because the law text the judges used allowed it. The king decided the surviving texts were corrupt and had a team of scholars check and copy them all. The final copies were stamped with three seals, a lion, an elephant lion and a crystal lotus, belonging to the three chief ministries, which gave the code its name.

The texts go back to Ayutthaya laws, which in turn drew on Indian law brought by the Mon and others. They are a key source for Ayutthaya's society, from slavery and debt to the ranks of officials. King Chulalongkorn's reforms began replacing them with Western style codes, the first in 1908. See Rattanakosin Kingdom.
